r: The Constitution provides only for the election of the Senate President and Speaker by a majority of all members; how other officers (including the minority leader) are chosen is for each House to decide. The Court will not intrude into this internal matter absent grave abuse. The Court took jurisdiction (whether the Constitution was violated is justiciable) but found no violation: senators who did not vote for the winning Senate President do not ipso facto form the ‘minority’, and no law or Senate rule makes the losing candidate the minority leader.
f: Senators who did not vote for the winning Senate President claimed the minority leadership belonged to the losing candidate.
x: Leadership fights in Congress (Speaker or Senate President changes in the news).

r: The House alone determines how its minority leader and other officers are chosen (Art. VI, Sec. 16(1) and (3)); the Court will not compel recognition of a particular minority leader. Mandamus does not lie. A ‘long-standing tradition’ that the runner-up for Speaker becomes minority leader creates no enforceable duty; the floor leader’s unobjected motion departing from it was validly adopted by the House.
f: Members who abstained or voted for others in the Speaker election claimed the minority leadership after the House recognized another group.
x: Pair with Santiago v. Guingona.

r: Quorum is a majority of the members within the coercive jurisdiction of the House. The Senate had 24 members; 12 is only half of 24 and not a majority, but one senator was abroad, beyond the Senate’s power to compel attendance, so the base was 23, and 12 is a majority of 23: a quorum. The walkout of Avelino’s group did not stop the 12 from continuing the session; the answer would differ had ten or fewer remained. The Court first refused jurisdiction (election of the Senate President is internal), then assumed it on reconsideration.
f: After Senate President Avelino walked out, 12 senators elected Cuenco as acting Senate President; one senator was in the US.
h: Cuenco’s election valid (on reconsideration the Court assumed jurisdiction and ruled on quorum).
x: Quorum disputes (absent, detained, or abroad members). Compare Jalosjos: absence due to lawful detention. Under the 1987 Constitution, quorum and the vote to elect are different: Sec. 16(1) requires the Senate President or Speaker to be elected by a majority of all the Members, so a 12-vote election in a 24-member Senate is open to attack even if 12 is a quorum under Avelino; argue both ways.
s: Quorum counts members within the coercive jurisdiction of the House.

r: The enrolled bill and the House Journal are conclusive that the TRAIN Law’s bicameral conference report was ratified with a quorum. Quorum is presumed to continue unless questioned through the House’s own procedures (roll call); unauthenticated videos and photos cannot overturn the Journal.
f: Three House members claimed the TRAIN Law (RA 10963) bicameral report was ratified late at night without a quorum.
x: Challenges to a law based on events on the floor (quorum, voting) — the enrolled bill and Journal control.
s: Enrolled bill and Journal are conclusive; quorum presumed unless questioned by roll call.

r: The Court may interpret and enforce legislative rules when the rights of third parties are affected. Under the CA’s rules, a motion to reconsider a confirmation that is never approved does not set the confirmation aside. Only a vote of the majority of the Commission’s members present can reopen a confirmation and recall it; it must be the act of the collective body, not of a single member.
f: A judge’s appointment was confirmed, then a member moved for reconsideration; the motion was never acted on, and the Secretary of Justice treated the confirmation as recalled.
h: The confirmation stood; Pacete was entitled to the office.
x: Exception to non-interference in internal rules: third-party rights.

r: Violation of internal House rules alone (as distinguished from constitutional requirements) is not grave abuse; rules are procedural and may be waived. The Court will not inquire behind the Speaker’s ruling and the enrolled bill absent a constitutional violation. Quoting Osmeña v. Pendatun: mere failure to conform to parliamentary usage does not invalidate an action when the requisite number of members have agreed to the measure.
f: Members claimed the sin tax law (RA 8240) was railroaded when the chair declared the bicameral report approved without allowing a question on quorum.
x: Use when a challenge rests only on breach of House or Senate rules. Distinguish Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole (constitutional requirements like quorum and publication are enforceable).
s: Violating internal rules alone is not grave abuse; rules may be waived.

r: Mandamus will not lie to compel the legislature to reinstate a member it suspended; the courts cannot control legislative discipline. The Court nonetheless conceded that the Senate exceeded its power: under the Jones Law it could punish an appointive senator for disorderly behavior but could not expel him, and a one-year suspension of an appointive member, which silences his district with no way to fill the seat, is a qualified expulsion. (Under the 1987 Constitution, suspension cannot exceed 60 days.)
f: The Senate suspended an appointive senator for one year for assaulting a colleague.
x: Historical baseline; note the 1987 Constitution now limits suspension to 60 days and requires a two-thirds vote. Johnson, dissenting: the resolution was an expulsion in effect, and the Court may rule on the legality of positive acts of another branch that deprive a person of rights; at least a declaration that it was ultra vires should issue. Treat the case as possibly bad law: there are no appointive legislators now, Osmeña v. Pendatun later upheld an inherent power to suspend elective members, the 1987 text expressly allows suspension (two-thirds, 60 days), and expanded judicial review (Art. VIII, Sec. 1) undercuts the ‘no power of coercion’ reasoning.

r: The speech and debate privilege protects members from being questioned elsewhere, not from discipline by their own House. What is ‘disorderly behavior’ is for the House to decide, and the Court will not review it; taking up other business before acting does not waive the House’s power to discipline (its rules may be waived). The 1935 Constitution mentioned only expulsion and set no limit on suspension, but the Court held the power to suspend is an inherent legislative prerogative the Constitution did not impair, and let the 15-month suspension stand; Alejandrino’s doubt about suspension concerned an appointive senator under the Jones Law. The privilege exists so members can speak with the fullest liberty, protected from the resentment of the powerful, but it is not absolute.
f: Rep. Osmeña accused President Garcia of bribery in a privilege speech; the House suspended him for 15 months.
x: The 2023 Teves question: the House’s power to discipline is broad, but the 1987 Constitution caps suspension at 60 days, requires two-thirds of all members to suspend or expel, and due process applies. A conviction is not required.
g: Gatmaytan’s book cites Osmeña for the court’s deference on what counts as disorderly behavior.
s: Speech privilege does not protect from one’s own House; what is disorderly is for the House.

r: The Sandiganbayan may order the preventive suspension of a member of Congress charged under RA 3019; it is not a penalty and so does not encroach on the House’s power to discipline. Separation of powers does not exempt legislators from the anti-graft law. It follows Santiago v. Sandiganbayan (2001), which upheld the 90-day preventive suspension of Senator Defensor Santiago for acts as immigration commissioner: suspension under Sec. 13 of RA 3019 is mandatory once a valid information is filed, and is a precautionary measure to keep the accused from intimidating witnesses, tampering with records or committing further malfeasance, distinct from the chamber’s power to discipline under Art. VI, Sec. 16(3).
f: The Sandiganbayan ordered the 90-day preventive suspension of Rep. Ceferino Paredes, Jr., charged under RA 3019; Speaker De Venecia and the House questioned the order as an intrusion into the House’s power to discipline its Members.
x: Distinguish preventive suspension by courts (precautionary) from discipline by the House (punitive). The two-thirds vote and the 60-day cap of Sec. 16(3) govern only the chamber’s own discipline, not a court’s preventive suspension (jurisprudence limits that to 90 days).

r: A senator’s insulting speech in the Senate is covered by parliamentary immunity; the Court will not discipline her as a lawyer for it. Her chamber is the proper body to discipline. The Court nonetheless criticized her language.
f: Senator Santiago, in a privilege speech, said she would ‘spit on the face’ of Justices and called the Court a court of ‘idiots’.
x: Speech and debate privilege versus discipline by courts.

n: Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole
r: The Senate has full discretion over its internal rules, subject to the Constitution: quorum, voting, and publication where required. The Committee of the Whole needed a quorum of a majority of the Senate, and its rules required publication before taking effect. The Senate’s rule-making is exempt from judicial interference except on a clear showing of arbitrary and improvident use amounting to a denial of due process. The Constitution does not require internal rules to be published unless the rules themselves say so; here Sec. 81, Rule 15 of the Committee’s rules made publication a condition of effectivity, so adopting the already-published Ethics Committee rules was not enough.
f: The Senate Committee of the Whole took over an ethics complaint against Senator Villar after the Ethics Committee was not constituted.
h: Referral to the Committee of the Whole upheld as an internal Senate matter, but the Committee had to publish its rules before proceeding, because its own rules required publication.
x: Constitutional limits on internal legislative proceedings: quorum, voting, publication, due process.

r: Enrolled bill doctrine: the signatures of the Senate President and the Speaker and the certification of the secretaries are conclusive of due enactment. Astorga does not apply absent a withdrawal of signatures. The doctrine rests on separation of powers: the Court must respect the legislative process of a coequal branch. It is court-made and has no express constitutional basis.
f: Challengers to the K-12 law claimed irregularities in its passage.
h: Enrolled bill doctrine applied; challenge on that point rejected.
x: Claims that a law was passed irregularly (readings, bicam changes).

sub: V.A.3 Probative value of the Journal
r: The legislative Journal is conclusive on what happened; the Court will not admit extrinsic evidence (e.g., that clocks were stopped) to show a law was passed after adjournment. Courts take judicial notice of the Journals; inquiring into their veracity would breach separation of powers, and public policy requires the authenticity of laws to rest on permanent public records rather than the uncertain memory of witnesses.
f: Pons, prosecuted for illegally importing opium under Act No. 2381, claimed the Act was passed on March 1, 1914, after the special session had legally ended at midnight of February 28, and offered evidence that the clock had been stopped; the Journals recorded adjournment sine die on February 28.
x: The Journal’s probative value.

r: It is approval by Congress, not the signatures, that makes a law. Where the Senate President and the President withdrew their signatures because the enrolled text was not what the Senate approved, there was no enrolled bill, and the Journal was consulted: the bill did not become law. The presiding officers’ certification does not add to a bill’s validity or cure a defect in its passage. The Journal is no ordinary record; the Constitution requires it, so it may be consulted to check whether the text signed by the President is the text both Houses passed.
f: The bill signed into law (RA 4065) omitted Senate floor amendments and contained a committee version instead.
x: The exception to the enrolled bill doctrine.
s: Approval by Congress, not the signatures, makes a law; with no valid enrolled bill, the Journal governs.

r: The enrolled bill is conclusive as to the text; for matters the Constitution does not require to be entered in the Journal, the enrolled bill prevails over the Journal. Errors are corrected by amendment, not by judicial decree.
f: A police chief applicant argued the enrolled Police Act omitted a phrase approved on the floor.
x: When the Journal may be consulted: only for matters the Constitution requires it to record (e.g., yeas and nays on third reading, veto messages).

r: A salary increase for members of Congress takes effect only after the expiration of the full term of all members of both Houses who approved it; the earliest effectivity is after both chambers’ members have completed their terms. ‘All the Members’ means both chambers together, so a new House could not enjoy the RA 4134 raise while senators who voted for it remained in office (it could not take effect before December 30, 1969). The delay is a deliberate deterrent against legislators voting themselves raises.
f: The 1965–1966 budget released increased salaries for House members before all senators who approved the increase had finished their terms.
x: Pay increases for legislators (Art. VI, Sec. 10).

r: A retiring member cannot compute retirement benefits on an increased salary he could not receive during his term; that would indirectly increase compensation in violation of the Constitution. A retirement gratuity is part of compensation within the constitutional prohibition.
f: A congressman retiring at the end of 1969 sought a gratuity based on a raise effective only for the next Congress.
x: Indirect increases in legislators’ compensation.

r: The privilege from arrest covers only offenses punishable by not more than six years while Congress is in session. A congressman convicted of a non-bailable crime cannot attend sessions; election does not exempt him from lawful confinement, and equal protection does not create a class of legislators. Voters elected him knowing he was confined; the popular mandate cannot override lawful restraints. Temporary leave from prison is allowed only for emergencies, and attending sessions and committee meetings five days a week is not an emergency and would make him a free man.
f: Rep. Jalosjos, convicted of statutory rape and detained, asked to attend House sessions.
x: Detained or arrested legislators (2013 Dimaporo item; Trillanes).
s: Arrest privilege covers offenses up to six years only; election does not free a convicted member.

r: Jalosjos applies to legislators under pre-trial detention for an offense punishable by reclusion perpetua where the evidence of guilt is strong. Election does not cure the restriction on liberty. That he was only a detention prisoner, not a convict, made no difference: detainees, like convicts, cannot hold office or practise a profession while detained (People v. Maceda), and the duties of high office are not a substantial distinction that lifts him out of the class of prisoners. Voters elected him knowing he could legislate only within prison confines.
f: Detained for the Oakwood mutiny (coup d’état), Trillanes won as senator and asked to attend sessions and hold office in detention.
x: Pair with Jalosjos.

r: ‘Speech or debate therein’ covers utterances in the performance of official functions (floor speeches, votes, bills, committee acts). An open letter published in newspapers during recess is not privileged.
f: A congressman released an open letter to the President alleging plots by army officers, published in newspapers while Congress was in recess.
h: Not privileged, but the letter was found not libelous; dismissal affirmed.
x: Is the statement within legislative function? Press releases and interviews are not (see Trillanes v. Castillo-Marigomen).
s: Speech privilege covers official legislative acts, not open letters or press releases.
test: Protected acts: (1) speeches on the floor while in session; (2) statements made or votes cast in the halls of Congress while in session; (3) bills introduced, whether in session or not; (4) other official acts, inside or outside Congress, in the official discharge of duties as members of Congress or of its committees.

r: Media interviews are not legislative acts and are not protected by the speech and debate clause; the privilege covers only what is necessary to the legislative process. The privilege attaches not because a lawmaker is speaking but because the statement is made in furtherance of legislation; talking to the press is an ordinary political activity, ‘political in nature, rather than legislative’.
f: A senator repeated his corruption accusations against a businessman in media interviews.
h: Not privileged; the libel suit could proceed.
x: Legislators speaking to the press or on social media.

r: A legislator may not hold another government office. By taking his oath as a member of the Batasan, a governor forfeited the governorship. The rule was the 1973 Constitution’s (Art. VIII, Sec. 10, as amended), which barred a Batasan member from any other government office during his tenure, the only exceptions being Prime Minister and Cabinet member; the 1987 Constitution keeps the bar (Art. VI, Sec. 13) but drops the Cabinet exception.
f: A provincial governor won a Batasan seat, took his oath, and still claimed the governorship.
x: Incompatible offices: accepting the legislative seat vacates the other office.

r: A legislator barred from appearing as counsel before an administrative body cannot do so indirectly by buying a few shares to intervene as a ‘stockholder’. A stockholder intervening for his own interest ordinarily does not appear as counsel; what made this an indirect appearance was the token stake (ten shares) bought after the fact, after his appearance as counsel had been objected to. Decided under Art. VIII, Sec. 11 of the 1973 Constitution, now Art. VI, Sec. 14.
f: An assemblyman bought ten shares of a corporation a day before seeking to intervene in an SEC case where he could not appear as counsel.
x: Art. VI, Sec. 14 cannot be circumvented.

r: A detained senator-petitioner’s wish to personally argue her own case must yield to the restrictions on her liberty from detention; the Court denied De Lima’s request to appear at oral arguments.
f: Senator De Lima, a petitioner in the ICC withdrawal case and detained on drug charges, asked to appear in person to argue.
x: Read with Art. VI, Sec. 14 (no personal appearance as counsel) and Jalosjos. She asked to appear as a party, not as counsel, so Sec. 14 was not the ground; the denial rested on her detention, and her co-petitioners (Senators Pangilinan and Drilon) could argue the case.

r: The PNRC chairmanship is not a government office or a GOCC position, so Senator Gordon did not forfeit his seat (2009). The 2009 ruling that RA 95 (PNRC charter) was unconstitutional as a special charter for a private corporation was reversed in 2011: the PNRC is sui generis, an auxiliary of government, and its validity was not the lis mota. Why the chairmanship is not a government office: the PNRC Chairman is elected by a private-sector-controlled Board and is not appointed by the President or any department head, so he is not a government official or employee.
f: Red Cross chapter officers asked the Court to declare Gordon’s Senate seat forfeited when he became PNRC chairman.
h: Gordon kept his seat; RA 95 provisions upheld on reconsideration. RA 10530 (2013) later recognized the PNRC as an independent, autonomous, non-governmental organization auxiliary to the authorities.
x: The 2024 midterm asked how RA 10530 cured the Liban issues: it settles the PNRC’s status by statute (not a GOCC, not a private corporation needing SEC registration), which also settles that a legislator may chair it.
test: Art. VI, Sec. 13: (1) incompatible office (any other government office or GOCC post: forfeits the seat); (2) forbidden office (any office created, or whose pay was increased, during the term: cannot be appointed at all).
s: PNRC chairmanship is not a government office; RA 95 upheld in 2011 (PNRC sui generis).
